lines: The Overview page arrives in about a second. The last two releases each took a piece out of this; what was left was the page adding up the same account totals sixteen times over to draw itself once.

The question about a newly arrived account no longer holds the rest of the application shut. It covers the screen on purpose, because who runs an account decides whether its balance is the firm's money or yours, but until now every click behind it did nothing at all and said nothing either, which looked like the application had stopped working. Click away from it, or press Later, and it steps aside. Neither answers it: the question comes back the next time your terminals are read.

Updating no longer closes the application and leaves it closed. Pressing Update shut the application down to make way for the installer, then stopped the installer along with it, so nothing was installed and nothing came back. If your copy has been sitting on an older version since the last time you tried to update, that is why.

The Overview page settles instead of working itself out over and over. Each time the application looked at your terminals, it told every open tab that the figures had moved, whether any of them had or not. So the page spent its time doing the sums again rather than showing them to you, and it got slower the more tabs you had open.

The Overview page appears straight away again. It was taking the better part of a minute, because drawing it once meant working out one account's day-by-day balance history a hundred times over. It is worked out once now. Nothing about the figures has changed.

**You can now place a hedge from the calculator.** Size it as before, then Arm and Fire, one button with a second between them. Both legs go to the two terminals you chose, each with its stop and its target on the broker's own server, and the application carries the pair to the end: if one leg is taken by the market it closes the other, and if you move a stop by hand on one leg the other follows. A line under the header follows the hedge while it is in the market, and you can close both legs from the page.
**Each terminal on Sources gains a choice of how it may be driven**, and says in plain words what it still needs before an order can go. Nothing is sent to a terminal you have not chosen a route for.

**Set this terminal up.** One press attaches the expert, turns on Algo Trading and turns on One Click Trading, and the terminal comes back ready in about twenty seconds. It lists everything it will do before it does any of it, and it never types into a login window. The same button starts a terminal you have closed, and offers to update the expert in one running an older version.

**The expert the application installs is a trading desk of its own.** Open at market or rest an order on a line you drag, with the stop and target placed for you; two chains of positions side by side, each with one stop and one target you drag on the chart; break even, risk free and save profit as buttons or as lines you set in advance; keyboard shortcuts; and limits on spread, size, margin and the day's loss. Five colour schemes, and a separate choice for each terminal. It leaves your chart exactly as it found it.
**The plan you arm is drawn on your prop chart** before anything is placed, with the risk and the reward shaded, and you can drag its entry line to move the whole plan without arming again.

**A position you open on the prop terminal yourself can be hedged for you.** Off by default. Turn it on and the matching leg goes to your broker at the ratio the calculator suggests, and the pair is carried like any other. What you already had open stays your own.

**You can hedge any instrument your brokers offer.** The application no longer has to have heard of it: it reads your Market Watch, and two brokers spelling one instrument differently are matched wherever the spelling allows. Where it cannot tell, it asks you once.
**Sources can make you a second terminal**, copied from one you already have, with a shortcut that starts it separately. It carries no account, no history and no saved login.
**Recording a plan now asks for the account the firm handed you**, and refuses one that was not opened at the plan's size. A plan nothing has happened under can be deleted rather than closed.
**A trade you place appears here in about a second** instead of up to half a minute, and the terminals page loads about twice as fast.

**Settings you change now take effect straight away.** How often the terminals are read, the quote windows, the clock drift limit and the history lookback were being saved and shown back to you without being used. Six more numbers are yours to set, and a new Execution tab holds every dial for driving a terminal.

Some figures were being worked out wrongly and are corrected, so a few numbers will read differently after this update. What execution costs is now measured on the instrument you are sizing rather than pooled across everything the account has traded, which was overstating a gold hedge by about thirty times. A plan's account no longer reports its whole drawdown allowance as spent because the application read it before the firm's money arrived.

Arming refuses, with the reason and what to do about it, when a leg has no stop, when a stop is on the wrong side of its entry, when the two legs face the same way, when the market has already moved past the plan, when the account is not the one a plan is running on, and when the position that opened is not the one that was ordered.
A window you have open in your terminal is never closed by the application. If one is open when a hedge is armed, it says which window it is and does nothing.
If the application stops while a hedge is being placed, it works out what actually reached the market when it comes back, rather than leaving that account unable to hedge again.

Closing a hedge no longer reports that the terminal refused when it did the work, and a hedge left armed on a driven terminal withdraws itself after half an hour and frees the account. You can change that time, or switch it off, under Settings, Execution.

Wherever an account appears it now names the plan it came from, and that name takes you to the plan. Six accounts of one firm used to be six identical rows, and which purchase each came from was on no screen.

When the application updates while you have a window of it open, that window says so and offers to reload. The message was there before, but only a corner of it reached the screen and the button was off the edge.
Several figures were being worked out wrongly and are corrected, so some numbers will read differently after this update. What each of them was doing is below.
Broker trading that answered no hedge was counting your hedged legs a second time. It read as a profit where the truth was a loss.
The spread your fills paid is now shown. It disappeared whenever a single operation was missing its quotes, and spread usually costs several times the commission.

A hedge that raised a question you had not answered kept its money out of your plans and your accounts until you accepted it. Both its legs were closed and the money was already yours, so it counts. The question stays on the row where you can read it.
The positions listed as having no counterpart on the Sources page counted trades that had been hedged all along.
A challenge account you have not put in a plan no longer has its chart drawn from zero, which showed the balance the firm opened it at as profit.

When your firm hands over the next account before it closes the one that passed, you can now record it against the plan it came from. There was no way to do that: the plan was still running, so nothing offered it, and recording a new purchase would have charged you a second fee and started the account over at the first stage. Every open plan is offered now, and one that is still running says which account joining it will mark as passed.

Each terminal lists the accounts it holds, not only the one it is logged into, and says which of them have never been read. Log into one and it is read on the next cycle. The page also loads about twice as fast.

Hedges are found wherever both their legs are stored, not only where a terminal happened to be pointed when they arrived. On a month of real trading that is the difference between finding a third of them and finding almost all.

Recording a pairing, declaring a trade as your own, accepting a hedge and confirming what a server is now take under a second. They used to take twenty to thirty, because each one opened MetaTrader for no reason.

A plan now shows what it has actually been worth: the price together with the broker money its hedges earned. It reads as the chain it is, from what you bought through every account it gained, and the Plans page charts them all side by side. Finished plans fold up.

The application works out for itself what happened to a challenge account. When the firm withdraws its right to trade, reaching the target passes the plan and crossing a drawdown floor closes it, named after the floor. You are asked only when the account is gone and none of its own figures explains why.

The daily drawdown floor is now drawn on the challenge chart, day by day, with the day an account went through it marked. It is rebuilt from your own trades, so it is there for accounts the application was never watching.
Each account shows one gauge, running from the floor that loses it to the target that passes it, instead of two bars that could not be read together.
When a new account appears on a terminal, the application says so wherever you are and asks the one thing it cannot work out: what the server is, or which plan the account came from.
Installing an update shows what it is doing from the moment you press the button until the application comes back. Before this the window simply closed and nothing happened until it was over.
Messages appear as cards under the header rather than a line of grey text, and anything refused stays on screen until you have read it.
Pairing a leg by hand is a clearer screen. The trade you are answering reads as one line, the closest candidate is already chosen, and you can see what the pairing would make before you record it.
The calculator no longer gets stuck when it is remembering an account you have since removed, and no longer blinks every time the terminals are read.
Every account now says whether you may still trade in it. The one your plan is running on is marked, and so are the ones that have passed or been lost.
Prop and broker accounts are told apart at a glance rather than by reading the word.
Reading the terminals now has its own small control inside the status pill at the top, so the bar that sat above the reports is gone. Export moved up beside the page title.
The button on an account that belongs to no plan used to do nothing at all. It now takes you to the form, and says what it does.
A challenge stage looks the same wherever it appears. In the calculator, the account you had chosen showed its stage in the wrong stage's colour.
When a new version is waiting, the About page now offers to install it, rather than only telling you it is there.
Closing Prop Hedge Reports from the tray now says so on the page, instead of leaving a tab that quietly stops keeping up.
You can leave that tab open. Start the app again and the page comes back on its own, where you left it.
